lesson.title: Inflation and Purchasing Power
lesson.summary: Why prices rise, how inflation erodes purchasing power, and who wins and loses.

blocks.text: Inflation is the generalized and continuous increase in prices over time. When inflation rises, each dollar buys less — purchasing power falls.

items: Excess demand: more money chasing the same goods
Supply shock: scarcity of inputs drives prices up
Expectations: if everyone expects inflation, it tends to become self-fulfilling

blocks.text: Debtors gain: their debts are worth less in real terms. Creditors and fixed-wage workers lose: their purchasing power falls. That is why central banks aim to keep inflation under control.
Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. — Milton Friedman

cards.back: A generalized and continuous increase in prices that reduces the purchasing power of each unit of currency.

cards.front: Why do debtors benefit from inflation?
cards.back: Because the real value of their debts decreases — they repay with money that is worth less than when they borrowed it.
It occurs when there is more money in circulation than goods available, causing prices to rise.

quiz.question: Who tends to be harmed by high inflation?
options: Owners of real assets like real estate
quiz.explanation: Workers with fixed wages lose purchasing power because their earnings don't keep up with rising prices.

quiz.question: What can cause supply-side inflation?
options: Scarcity of raw materials or energy
quiz.explanation: When essential inputs become scarce or more expensive, production costs rise and final prices follow.
